Puzzle 14 · 15 of 16

What Compose actually shares

One set of Compose UI code runs on Android and on iOS. "Same code" hides three layers. Here's which ones are shared, and the one that's written again for every platform.

  • Puzzle 1: What every target has

    Code lives in source sets. commonMain is compiled for every target, so it may only use what every target has; androidMain and iosMain are compiled for one platform each and can use that platform's own APIs.

  • Puzzle 13: Compose in one puzzle

    In Compose, a screen is a Kotlin function marked @Composable that describes the UI for the current data, instead of creating and updating view objects. When that data, its state, changes, Compose calls the affected functions again: recomposition. remember keeps a value across those calls. A compiler plugin rewrites every @Composable function so the runtime can track what each one showed and redo only what changed.

Starting from zero? The blocks under this puzzle are 3 puzzles: 0 → 1 → 13. Know them already? Start here.

The problem

You wrote a @Composable screen in commonMain. On Android it shows your list; on an iPhone it shows the same list. But Jetpack Compose was built for Android: it draws through Android's own screen classes and reads Android touch events. So what exactly runs on the iPhone, and which part had to be written again?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

Think of Compose as three layers.

At the bottom, the Compose runtime and the Compose compiler plugin. The compiler turns your @Composable functions into code that records what they showed. The runtime tracks state, such as what you remember, and decides what to recompose when it changes. Neither knows anything about pixels or Android, and Compose Multiplatform shares both with Jetpack Compose.

In the middle, the libraries you call: ui, foundation, material3. Text, Column, LazyColumn and Modifier are the same APIs on every target. On Android your build uses Google's Jetpack Compose artifacts. On iOS, desktop and web it uses JetBrains' builds of the same libraries. The Gradle plugin picks for you.

At the top, the platform layer: the part written per target. It's the window your UI lives in, how touches arrive, the surface the UI is drawn onto, the keyboard and text input, and what accessibility tools such as VoiceOver, iOS's screen reader, are told. That's the thin part JetBrains rewrote for iOS, and it's where platform differences show.

Some APIs never leave Android: anything that needs a Context, such as LocalContext, or Android resources through R. They stay in androidMain.

The analogy

A play staged in two theatres. The script and the actors (runtime and libraries) travel. Each theatre has its own stage, lights and doors (the platform layer), so the same scene can feel slightly different in each.

Check yourself

Your app targets Android and iOS with Compose Multiplatform. Which build of material3 does the Android app use?

Right. Android gets Google's artifacts.

Not quite. material3 is available from common code on all targets.

Not quite. On Android the build switches to Google's artifacts; JetBrains' builds are for the other targets.

Which part of Compose had to be rewritten to run on iOS?

Right. Only the top layer is per platform.

Not quite. Your composables are common code; they run unchanged.

Not quite. The runtime is shared; puzzle 9 showed Kotlin/Native has its own GC.

What's the difference between the Compose runtime and the platform layer?

Right. State vs pixels and input.

Not quite. It's the other way round: the runtime knows nothing about pixels.

Sources
  • Kotlin docs: Compose Multiplatform and Jetpack Compose ("It shares the Compose compiler and runtime with Jetpack Compose and uses the same APIs"; "When you build your Compose Multiplatform application for Android, you use the Jetpack Compose artifacts published by Google. For example, if you add compose.material3 to your dependencies, your project will use androidx.compose.material3:material3 in the Android target, and org.jetbrains.compose.material3:material3 in other targets.")

What you now know

Compose Multiplatform shares the Compose compiler and runtime with Jetpack Compose, and the same APIs. On Android your build uses Google's Jetpack Compose artifacts; on iOS, desktop and web it uses JetBrains' builds of the same libraries. What's written per target is the platform layer: window, touches, drawing surface, text input and accessibility.
